The Yangtze River is the longest and most economically important river in [Asia](/wiki/Asia "Asia") and the fifth largest in the world in terms of flow. It is also the largest river entirely within a single country. Its estuary had an estimated annual flow of 995.8 cubic kilometers per year (31,550 m3/s) between 1955 and 2021.
The last gauging station on the river is at [Datong](/wiki/Tongling "Tongling") ([30°50′57.9192″N 117°43′47.4096″E﻿ / ﻿30.849422000°N 117.729836000°E﻿ / 30.849422000; 117.729836000](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Yangtze&params=30_50_57.9192_N_117_43_47.4096_E_)). At this location, the water flow is regularly monitored. The chart below is based on average flows between 1950 and 2020.[[1]](#cite_note-Evolution_of_the_main_channel_of_the_Yangtze_River-1)[[95]](#cite_note-The_BOH-95)[[2]](#cite_note-Sediment_sink-source_transitions_in_the_middle_and_lower_reaches_of_the_Yangtze_River_estuary-2)

2000 Summer Olympics :: The Games :: Costs :: chunk_0003
The *Oxford Olympics Study 2016* estimates the outturn cost of the Sydney 2000 Summer Olympics at US$5 billion in 2015 dollars and cost overrun at 90% in real terms.[[9]](#cite_note-10) This includes sports-related costs only; that is, (i) *operational costs* incurred by the organising committee to stage the Games, e.g., expenditures for technology, transportation, workforce, administration, security, catering, ceremonies, and medical services, and (ii) *direct capital costs* incurred by the host city and country or private investors to build; e.g., the competition venues, the Olympic village, international broadcast centre, and media and press centre, which are required to host the Games. Indirect capital costs are *not* included, such as for road, [rail](/wiki/Olympic_Park_railway_line,_Sydney "Olympic Park railway line, Sydney"), airport infrastructure, hotel upgrades, or other business investments incurred in preparation for the Games but not directly related to staging the Games. The cost for Sydney 2000 compares with a cost of US$4.6 billion for Rio 2016, US$40‍–‍44 billion for Beijing 2008, and US$51 billion for Sochi 2014, the most expensive Olympics in history. The average cost for the Summer Games since 1960 is US$5.2 billion, average cost overrun is 176%.

In 2000, the [Auditor-General of New South Wales](/wiki/Auditor-General_of_New_South_Wales "Auditor-General of New South Wales") reported that the Sydney Games cost [A$](/wiki/A$ "A$")6.6 billion, with a net cost to the public between A$1.7 and A$2.4 billion.[[10]](#cite_note-11)[[11]](#cite_note-12) In the years leading up to the Games, funds were shifted from education and health programs to cover Olympic expenses.[[12]](#cite_note-FindlingPelle2004-13)

See also: [Afrotropical realm](/wiki/Afrotropical_realm "Afrotropical realm") and [Palearctic realm](/wiki/Palearctic_realm "Palearctic realm")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/58/Vegetation_Africa.png/330px-Vegetation_Africa.png)](/wiki/File:Vegetation_Africa.png)

The main biomes in Africa

Africa has over 3,000 [protected areas](/wiki/Protected_area "Protected area"), with 198 marine protected areas, 50 biosphere reserves, and 80 wetlands reserves. Significant habitat destruction, increases in human population and poaching are reducing Africa's biological diversity and [arable land](/wiki/Arable_land "Arable land"). Human encroachment, civil unrest and the introduction of non-native species threaten biodiversity in Africa. This has been exacerbated by administrative problems, inadequate personnel and funding problems.[[160]](#cite_note-environmentalatlas-168)

[Deforestation](/wiki/Deforestation "Deforestation") is affecting Africa at twice the world rate, according to the United Nations Environment Programme ([UNEP](/wiki/UNEP "UNEP")).[[168]](#cite_note-176) The deforestation rate of 4.08 million hectares in 2000–2015 declined to 3.45 million ha per year in 2015–2025.[[169]](#cite_note-177) According to the University of Pennsylvania African Studies Center, 31% of Africa's pasture lands and 19% of its forests and woodlands are classified as degraded, and Africa is losing over four million hectares of forest per year, which is twice the average deforestation rate for the rest of the world.[[160]](#cite_note-environmentalatlas-168) Some sources claim that approximately 90% of the original, virgin forests in West Africa have been destroyed.[[170]](#cite_note-178) Over 90% of [Madagascar](/wiki/Madagascar "Madagascar")'s original forests have been destroyed since the arrival of humans 2000 years ago.[[171]](#cite_note-179) About 65% of Africa's agricultural land suffers from [soil d

On February 3, 2003, Burrell signed a six-year, $50 million contract with the Phillies.[[47]](#cite_note-47) He had two home runs and five RBI (including the game-winner) on April 9 in a 16–2 victory over the Braves.[[48]](#cite_note-48) The home runs both came against [Greg Maddux](/wiki/Greg_Maddux "Greg Maddux"), making Burrell the sixth player to hit two home runs in a game against Maddux (and the first since Rolen did it in 2001).[[6]](#cite_note-MLB-6) On May 20, he hit two home runs and had four RBI in an 11–7 victory over the Mets.[[49]](#cite_note-49) On August 9, Burrell hit a game-tying solo home run and a game-winning two-run home run in the 8th and 10th innings of an 8–6 victory over the [San Francisco Giants](/wiki/San_Francisco_Giants "San Francisco Giants").[[50]](#cite_note-50) He hit two home runs (including his 100th) on August 22 in a 9–4 victory over the [St. Louis Cardinals](/wiki/St._Louis_Cardinals "St. Louis Cardinals").[[51]](#cite_note-benching-51) On September 28, he had the final hit in [Veterans Stadium](/wiki/Veterans_Stadium "Veterans Stadium") (a single against [Jason Marquis](/wiki/Jason_Marquis "Jason Marquis")) in a 5–2 loss to Atlanta.[[6]](#cite_note-MLB-6)[[52]](#cite_note-52) Burrell endured a season-long [slump](/wiki/Slump_(sports) "Slump (sports)"), and he was occasionally benched for a few games (often in favor of [Ricky Ledée](/wiki/Ricky_Led%C3%A9e "Ricky Ledée")) by Phillies' manager [Larry Bowa](/wiki/Larry_Bowa "Larry Bowa").[[6]](#cite_note-MLB-6)[[51]](#cite_note-benching-51)[[53]](#cite_note-53) In 146 games, he batted .209 with 21 home runs and 64 RBI. However, his 21 home runs were still the second-highest total on the Phillies (teammate [Jim Thome](/wiki/Jim_Thome "Jim Thome") led the NL with 47).[[6]](#cite_note-MLB-6)[[54]](#cite_note-54)

Pittsburgh's rivalry with the [Baltimore Ravens](/wiki/Baltimore_Ravens "Baltimore Ravens") has had several memorable matchups and has escalated into a fierce competitive sports rivalry. The rivalry features the league's two longest tenure coaches Mike Tomlin and Raven's coach [John Harbaugh](/wiki/John_Harbaugh "John Harbaugh"). Both teams handed the other their first losses at their current home stadiums. The Steelers won the inaugural game played at [Baltimore's](/wiki/Baltimore,_Maryland "Baltimore, Maryland") [M&T Bank Stadium](/wiki/M%26T_Bank_Stadium "M&T Bank Stadium") in [1998](/wiki/1998_NFL_season "1998 NFL season"), 20–13, and three years later the [Ravens](/wiki/Baltimore_Ravens "Baltimore Ravens") handed the Steelers their first-ever loss at [Heinz Field](/wiki/Heinz_Field "Heinz Field"), 13–10. Later that season ([2001](/wiki/2001_NFL_season "2001 NFL season")) Pittsburgh won a [divisional playoff game](/wiki/2001%E2%80%9302_NFL_playoffs#AFC:_Pittsburgh_Steelers_27,_Baltimore_Ravens_10 "2001–02 NFL playoffs") 27–10 against Baltimore, who was the [defending Super Bowl champion](/wiki/Super_Bowl_XXXV "Super Bowl XXXV"). During their NFL championship season in [2000](/wiki/2000_Baltimore_Ravens_season "2000 Baltimore Ravens season"), the Ravens defeated the Steelers [in Pittsburgh](/wiki/Three_Rivers_Stadium "Three Rivers Stadium"), 16–0, in the season opener with the Steelers later exacting revenge, 9–6, in Baltimore (the Ravens' final loss of the season). During the Steelers 2008 Championship run, they beat the Ravens three times, including a win in the AFC Championship game. **English** is a [West Germanic language](/wiki/West_Germanic_languages "West Germanic languages") of the [Indo-European](/wiki/Indo-European_languages "Indo-European languages") language family that emerged in [early medieval England](/wiki/History_of_Anglo-Saxon_England "History of Anglo-Saxon England") and has since become a global [lingua franca](/wiki/Lingua_franca "Lingua franca").[[4]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThe_Routes_of_English-4)[[5]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrystal2003a6-5)[[6]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWardhaugh201055-6) The namesake of the language is the [Angles](/wiki/Angles_(tribe) "Angles (tribe)"), one of the [Germanic peoples](/wiki/Germanic_peoples "Germanic peoples") who [migrated to Britain](/wiki/Anglo-Saxon_settlement_of_Britain "Anglo-Saxon settlement of Britain") after the [end of Roman rule](/wiki/End_of_Roman_rule_in_Britain "End of Roman rule in Britain"). English is the [most spoken language](/wiki/List_of_languages_by_total_number_of_speakers "List of languages by total number of speakers") in the world, primarily due to the global influences of the former [British Empire](/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire") (succeeded by the [Commonwealth of Nations](/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Nations "Commonwealth of Nations")) and the [United States](/wiki/United_States "United States"). It is the most widely learned [second language](/wiki/Second_language "Second language") in the world, with more second-language speakers than native speakers. However, English is only the [third-most spoken native language](/wiki/List_of_languages_by_number_of_native_speakers "List of languages by number of native speakers"), after [Mandarin Chinese](/wiki/Mandarin_Chinese "Mandarin Chinese") and [Spanish](/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language").[[3]](#cite_note-Ethnologue26-3)
